odeComponent.htmlView:
Healing Music: Matching Music to Patient Needs



Music can create connection, comfort, distraction, and support, but the most important part of the experience is the human connection.

In this module, you'll explore how a patient's condition, needs, preferences, and environment can influence the music selected during a session.

You'll practice:

  • Recognizing important patient and environmental considerations
  • Matching musical approaches to patient conditions
  • Identifying characteristics of rhythmic, arrhythmic, and improvised music
  • Applying these concepts to realistic patient situations

odeComponent.htmlView:
Before choosing a piece of music, start with the person in front of you.

The practitioner's role is not simply to play music. It is to be present, observe, listen, and respond to what the patient needs.

Patients may have different preferences. Some may prefer familiar, quiet music. Others may want something more upbeat.

The appropriate choice begins with paying attention to the patient.

Listen to what the patient needs.

Who Else Can Hear the Music?

odeComponent.htmlView:
Who Else Can Hear the Music?


Music does not stop at the patient's bedside.

Before beginning a session, consider everyone who may hear the music.

This may include:

  • Other patients sharing the room
  • Family members
  • Visitors
  • Physicians and other healthcare providers
  • Hospital staff


Sound travels.

The music should be appropriate for the environment and for the people who may be affected by it.

odePagStructure.blockName: Section 2: Be Aware of the Environment

odeComponent.htmlView:
Consider the Lyrics


If you are playing a song with lyrics, consider what those lyrics communicate.

Some topics may be emotionally difficult or inappropriate for a particular setting.

Be aware of lyrics involving topics such as:

  • Self-harm
  • Death
  • Loss of a loved one
  • Other heavy or emotionally sensitive subjects


The goal is not simply to choose music the practitioner enjoys. The selection should be appropriate for the patient and the surrounding environment.

odePagStructure.blockName: Section 3: Beginning and Ending the Session

odeComponent.htmlView:
Begin With Silence


A music session does not have to begin with music. Start with silence.

Then:

  1. Begin gently.
  2. Play the first chord.
  3. Allow it to ring out for an extended period.
  4. Gradually lean into the piece.
  5. Incorporate silence into the music.


A gentle beginning can be especially important for patients who are sensitive to sound or sudden changes.

Give the patient time to enter the musical experience.

odePagStructure.blockName: Section 3: Beginning and Ending the Session

odeComponent.htmlView:
The ending of a session does not necessarily require immediate conversation.

After the music ends, silence can give the patient time to process what was given to them.

Speaking with the patient afterward can also provide an opportunity for connection and reflection.

The session can end with music, silence, conversation or a combination of the three.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Actively Dying Patients

Music for a patient who is actively dying may be used as transition support.

This approach uses improvisation and may be arrhythmic.

The practitioner should remain attentive to the patient and respond to what is happening in the moment.


Key idea:

Actively dying → Transition support → Improvisation / arrhythmic music


Transitioning music is typically improvised and contains the following characteristics:

Free improvisation
No fixed meter
Long sustained tones
Sparse melodic phrases
Extended pauses
Responding to the patient's breathing
Gradually changing musical texture


Song Example:

Click on the link below to listen to an improvised piece for bedside:

Listen to audio named "Arrhythmic Improvisation".

https://www.harppeacegiver.com/listen-to-examples

*Listen for how the music responds to the patient rather than imposing a fixed rhythm or structure. Improvisation may be arrhythmic, with pauses and changes that follow the patient's breathing and condition.
